capabilities.title: Register external model endpoints behind the same catalog and controls
capabilities.summary:
- **Discovery validates before it registers.** `discover_external_endpoint` validates the endpoint URL, authenticates with the supplied credential, and probes the provider's model inventory, returning the advertised model list for the operator to select from. Failures come back as classified discovery errors (unreachable, auth, malformed response), not generic 500s. The probe deliberately refuses to follow redirects, so the host that is validated and credentialed is the host the operator entered — a provider response cannot redirect the probe onward to a different address. This document claims the no-redirect behavior itself; it does not claim a general egress or private-address policy, which is a deployment network concern.
- **Credentials are handled server-side.** A stored credential can be referenced by secret URN instead of pasting a plaintext key; the URN is resolved server-side and the plaintext is used in memory for the probe — it is never returned to the client. The wizard offers existing-credential reuse when one is already stored for the endpoint.
- **Provider breadth through one wizard.** One wizard, entered from a vendor picker (AWS, Azure, LiteLLM, OpenAI, Other), covers two flows. The three-step discovery flow (source, setup, review) covers OpenAI directly; Azure OpenAI Service and Azure AI Foundry, with the Azure handler detected from the pasted hostname; and any OpenAI-compatible host — LiteLLM proxies, self-hosted vLLM, Ollama — with provider-specific inventory augmentation for LiteLLM and OpenRouter hosts. The two-step AWS flow (source, setup) covers AWS Bedrock (Claude, Nova, Llama 3, and other Bedrock-hosted families, every one dispatched through the Bedrock Converse API, with IAM access key or Bedrock API key auth, and an optional endpoint override for PrivateLink or non-commercial partitions) and AWS Transcribe (batch and streaming speech-to-text with S3 staging). Neither AWS flow discovers models. Bedrock requires a region and model or inference-profile identifier. Transcribe uses the fixed repo_modelId aws-transcribe; its form takes a display name, region, S3 bucket, credentials, and optional language code.
- **Registered models are ordinary models afterwards.** Selected models register into the catalog (with a per-model display name, description and purpose — chat, embedding or transcription — set at review time), deploy through the normal deployment lifecycle, and are listed by the deployment's `/v1/models` route. Applications then call them without knowing which provider sits behind them, because the request shape is the provider-agnostic OpenAI one. Which OpenAI-compatible operation a registered model answers follows the engine it was registered under, not this registration path — an `external_chat` model answers chat completions, while `external_embedding` and `external_transcribe` models answer their own operations. This document does not claim that every externally registered model exposes chat completions; the operation each engine answers is described with the serving surface (`models.openai-compatible-inference`), not here.
- **External engines are explicit, never guessed.** The external engine names (`external_chat`, `external_embedding`, `external_transcribe`) are part of the platform's canonical engine set but are registered explicitly through this path — automatic engine selection never returns them, so a local deploy cannot silently become an external one.
conditions: Outbound HTTPS from the Kamiwaza control plane to the provider hostname is permitted.
The operator holds a valid provider credential (API key, Azure resource or project key, AWS IAM access key or Bedrock bearer token, LiteLLM master key, or similar).
Registering a model (POST /models/) is admin-only; the discovery probe (POST /serving/external-endpoints/discover) requires only an authenticated user.
limits:
- Discovery requires the provider to be reachable and the credential to be enabled for the target models; for Azure, the deployment must exist in the project the URL points at. Egress-restricted networks must permit the provider hostnames (and for AWS Transcribe streaming, the separate streaming hostname and port).
- The wizard registers and Kamiwaza proxies; model quality, quota, and availability remain properties of the provider account. Testing each deployment from the Models list before applications call it is the documented practice.
- Serving external models through the OpenAI-compatible surface is claimed and evidenced separately as `models.openai-compatible-inference`.
- **Bedrock is Converse-only.** The `aws_bedrock` handler builds one LiteLLM call against `bedrock/converse/<model id>` for both credential types; there is no InvokeModel dispatch. Earlier revisions of this document repeated the public Bedrock guide's "Converse and InvokeModel APIs" wording; the handler source does not support the InvokeModel half, so it is recorded under `not_supported` rather than claimed.
- **Review-time customization is identity, not parameters.** The review step sets each selected model's display name, description and purpose. It writes an empty `system_config` and no default generation parameters; an earlier revision of this document claimed "default-parameter customization at review time", which the review step at the declared revision does not provide.
- **Registration and discovery have different gates.** Registering a model is admin-only on the API; the discovery probe itself is open to any authenticated user.

capabilities.title: Control model placement across hardware classes, including fractional GPU serving
capabilities.summary:
- estimate-model-vram
- place-deployment
- reserve-memory-budget
- classify-hardware
- serve-fractionally
- disable-fractional-sharing
- report-no-fit
- inspect-placement
conditions: The cluster exposes accelerator nodes with the labels placement classifies from, and the serving stack is installed.
limits:
- On managed clusters, placement respects whatever GPU sharing the cluster admin configured through the GPU Operator (MIG partitions, time-slicing, MPS) and requires no privileged access beyond the one-time install steps (a CRD and a read-only role for node labels). Without a configured sharing strategy, deployments still work but density is limited to one model per GPU.
- On hardware-isolated cards, capacity is the partition size, not the card: a model larger than the largest configured partition fails with a structured no-fit error even when the card as a whole is big enough.
- macOS installs run the control plane in a VM while model processes run natively on the host for Metal GPU access; they appear as standalone topology with the `metal_spawner` sharing class.
- **The placement details are empty on the default path.** The placement fields are nullable and written only from the operator's status, so a deployment made with operator emission off reports no topology, node, GPU index, class or allocated capacity.
- **The size of the unified-memory reserve is not established as one number.** The public fractional-serving guide states an 8 GiB operating-system reserve "before the budget is advertised", and core reports unified-memory metrics with an 8 GiB reserve (`UMA_RESERVE_GIB`, `kamiwaza/lib/gpu.py:13`). The placement planner at the declared operators revision instead subtracts a 4 GB system overhead from the advertised unified pool, plus 1 GB per deployment (`internal/controller/serving/planner/planner.go:36-48`, `planHCUMA`). Whether the advertised pool already has 8 GiB held back depends on the VRAM plugin, whose source is not in the reviewed set. Do not quote a specific reserve from this document.
- **Discrete shared GPUs carry no system reserve.** On a software-shared card with the VRAM plugin advertising, the planner fits the request plus 1 GB per-deployment overhead against the card's capacity less what other deployments hold (`planHCDS`).
- **The estimator degrades to a default response.** When no estimate can be produced, `estimate_model_vram` returns a default response rather than an error, so a caller cannot tell a failed estimate from a real one by status code alone.
- **A no-fit is a statement about tracked budgets.** Budgets count what Kamiwaza deployments reserved; the public guide notes that memory used by other processes is not tracked, so a model that fit at scheduling time can still run out of memory at load.
- The `surface` front matter above declares UI and API, while the estimator guarantee names the SDK method `client.serving.estimate_model_vram()`. The declared value is reproduced verbatim from the 2026-08-09 inventory run and is left as recorded rather than corrected here, so a consumer reading `surface` should not infer that the SDK estimator is unavailable. Reconciling the declaration is a change for the inventory's next pass.

capabilities.title: Serve CPU and NVIDIA GPU models on a restricted tenant install from owner-signed compute profiles
capabilities.summary:
- **Owner:** detect hardware facts, sign and publish the compute-profile bundle and optionally publish recipe catalogs that pin model configurations (the owner tool in the Kamiwaza core image; the kamiwaza-kubernetes-setup scripts are deprecated), and optionally install the owner admission webhook that protects the bundle ConfigMaps (kamiwaza-kubernetes-setup; its README heads that service "not yet cluster-qualified", so bundle integrity rests on the signature and the immutable-ConfigMap check, and both rest on the owner controlling the release's verifier settings).
- **Tenant:** deploy a CPU, GPU or (NVIDIA amd64) diffusion model through the normal deploy API, UI or SDK. Deploying remains a Kamiwaza-admin operation. A request needs no allocation block: the shipped UI sends none and core derives one. An explicit `inferenceResources` request can be sent through the API and, at the declared SDK revision, through the SDK (`deploy_model(..., inference_resources=...)`). The ui-v2 console's code can pass a block too, but only `frontend/` carries an image build at this revision.
- **Platform:** verify the bundle (signature, binding, namespace, version floor, expiry) before every sizing and dispatch, and refuse with a named reason when a check fails.
conditions: Off by default. The owner enables core.inferenceResources (enabled: true) and must then supply ownerPublicKey and clusterBindingId; the chart schema refuses enabled without them.

The cluster owner publishes an Ed25519-signed compute-profile bundle as an immutable ConfigMap in the tenant namespace, using the owner tool shipped in the Kamiwaza core image (python -m kamiwaza.serving.inference_resources.owner_tool: detect, keygen, pubkey, sign, render-catalog). The kamiwaza-kubernetes-setup owner scripts still work but are deprecated there and marked for removal in 1.4.0; on AMD hosts that repository's detector remains the only one, because the core image carries no rocminfo. Core refuses a bundle that fails the Ed25519 signature check against ownerPublicKey, names another clusterBindingId or namespace, is below the configured version floor or outside its validity window, or sits in a mutable ConfigMap. Those checks bind the tenant only while core's verifier settings stay owner-controlled: ownerPublicKey and clusterBindingId are values of the namespaced Helm release, and the setup repository's owner admission guide (docs/owner-inference-admission.md) states that the admission webhook does not stop a namespace administrator from replacing verifier settings, workload images or Pods, so a tenant that runs the release as namespace admin can point core at a key of its own. The checks also do not stop deletion or recreation of the bundle ConfigMap: that guide's acceptance test for the webhook is that tenant create, metadata update and delete on the bundle name are denied, and in the direct extension-runtime mode (the umbrella chart default) the core API role is itself granted ConfigMap create, update and delete. Write-protection of the bundle therefore depends on that webhook, which the setup repository's scripts README heads 'not yet cluster-qualified'.

The bundle must match the owner-profile schema this core revision vendors (kamiwaza/serving/inference_resources/inference-profiles.v1.schema.json, SHA-256 5cf3a6d3...7727e, byte-identical to the setup repository's copy at 0c3f08a9). At this revision that schema admits the optional accelerator.cudaDriverMajor fact (an integer from 11 to 99), and the core image's detector attests it by default. Rollback hazard: a core build without that schema (the public guide says any release earlier than 1.3.0; the setup repository adds a 1.3.0 build from before ENG-12867) rejects a bundle carrying the fact as a whole, so every tenant deployment fails authorization, CPU deployments included. Before rolling back, publish a signed revision without the fact.

At the declared revision the engine catalog publishes NVIDIA llama.cpp images for CUDA 13 (compute capability 7.5 or newer) and CUDA 12 (7.0 or newer) on amd64 and arm64, one vLLM image (CUDA 13, amd64, 7.5 or newer, and the engine requires bf16), and one diffusion image (CUDA 12, amd64, 8.0 or newer, and the engine requires bf16). For each NVIDIA binding core selects the newest image that both the attested compute capability and the attested driver CUDA major (cudaDriverMajor) can run. A binding that attests no driver major is not judged by one: the public guide records that a Turing-or-newer card on a CUDA 12 (R570) host is then given the CUDA 13 llama.cpp image, which exits at startup, and that an unattested vLLM binding fails the same way. Pascal and older cards have no image. The public guide states the diffusion image is not qualified below an R570 driver and that the platform does not refuse it there.
Preview. The public owner guide states live qualification covers k0s Kubernetes 1.36 only and that the page is 'not evidence of qualification'.
limits:
- **Off by default at every layer.** `InferenceResourceSettings.enabled` defaults to `False` and the core chart sets `inferenceResources.enabled: false`. Without the owner's public key and cluster binding id, the chart schema refuses `enabled: true`.
- **Not in the release candidate examined earlier (historical).** `delivery/1.3.0-rc.pre1.7/core-source` (`db335158b`) contains no `inference_resources` package: the tagged commit sits on a line that forked from develop (at `aeffeecdf`) before the merge that introduced it (kamiwaza#2819) and never took that merge in. Later release candidates were not examined. A 1.3.0 answer must say which build it is answering for.
- **Preview.** The public owner guide calls itself "a public owner reference, not evidence of qualification" and limits live qualification to k0s Kubernetes 1.36. The guide says chart, API and client contract checks cover Kubernetes 1.28 through 1.36, and that passing one "is not a live support claim".
- **Engines are the shipped catalog.** At the declared revision: llama.cpp (CPU and NVIDIA, amd64 and arm64), vLLM (NVIDIA amd64), diffusion (NVIDIA amd64) and whisper.cpp (CPU). Anything else is refused as "not qualified in this release". llama.cpp ships CUDA 13 and CUDA 12 NVIDIA builds and needs compute capability 7.0 or newer (7.5 for the CUDA 13 build); vLLM ships a CUDA 13 build only and needs 7.5 or newer with bf16; diffusion ships a CUDA 12 build only and needs 8.0 or newer with bf16.
- **The driver is judged only if the owner attests it.** Core picks the newest build the attested compute capability and the attested `cudaDriverMajor` both allow, and refuses when none fits. A binding that attests no driver major is given the newest build its card allows; on a CUDA 12 host that is a CUDA 13 llama.cpp or vLLM image that fails at startup. The core image's detector attests the fact by default; re-detect and re-sign after any driver change.
- **Tenant diffusion is one base pipeline on one device.** The model must be a diffusers repository with `model_index.json`; a single-file checkpoint, LoRA or Lightning adapters, a configured stream profile, `trust_remote_code`, DFloat11 models or settings, and more than one device are refused with the reason. The public guide says the diffusion image is not qualified below an R570 driver, and the platform does not enforce that.
- **Owner bundles must match this core's schema.** The schema vendored in core at the declared revision admits the optional `accelerator.cudaDriverMajor` fact. A core build from before that change closes the `accelerator` block without it and rejects the whole bundle, CPU deployments included; before rolling core back to such a build, publish a signed revision without the fact.
- **Tensor parallelism** is limited to whole-device bindings with an attested peer-to-peer path, up to 8 devices in one Pod on one node. The public owner guide records a deployment that spans more than one device as "implemented but not qualified live". The peer-path requirement is enforced on the path deployments take; an older, unused resolver in the same module still accepts a whole-device binding that attests no hardware facts, which `models.tensor-parallel-serving` records as an open defect. General (non-tenant) tensor parallelism is also described there.
- **The signed profiles bind the tenant only if the owner controls the release.** The verifying key (`ownerPublicKey`) and `clusterBindingId` are values of the namespaced Helm release; the setup repository's owner admission guide states that the webhook does not stop a namespace administrator from replacing verifier settings, workload images or Pods.
- **Accounted shares are bookkeeping, not isolation**, and the platform cannot detect a whole-device binding and an accounted binding overlapping on one GPU (ENG-12534); the owner must partition devices between them.
- **Key rotation is manual** (ENG-12500): a documented procedure in the deploy repository that restarts every trust-anchor consumer.
- **Deploying stays admin-only.** Namespace-admin permissions in Kubernetes do not grant the Kamiwaza `admin` role; the deploy route requires it.
- **External endpoints allocate nothing on a tenant cluster.** They are not sized and create no workload; an external-endpoint request that supplies an `inferenceResources` block, or a nonzero `gpu_allocation` or `vram_allocation`, is refused with HTTP 422.

capabilities.title: Serve models on an SSH-paired second GPU node
capabilities.summary:
- attach a paired node (`POST /cluster/attach_pairing`)
- detach the paired node (`POST /cluster/detach_pairing`)
- start model containers on the paired node (vLLM two-node Ray worker, llama.cpp)
- sync downloaded model files to the paired node
- report the paired node and its GPU inventory in cluster capabilities
conditions: The required configuration, services and permissions described below must be present.
limits:
Off until an administrator attaches a node. There is no separate feature flag: the settings are disabled when no remote host is stored (`kamiwaza/serving/two_node.py:190`), and the dataclass default is `enabled: bool = False` (`kamiwaza/serving/two_node.py:96`). The attach and detach routes are on the cluster router, which every install mounts (`kamiwaza/app.py:738`). Both routes require the admin role (`kamiwaza/cluster/api.py:64`). Setting `KAMIWAZA_PAIRED_NODE` in the API environment also attaches a node, after the same SSH check, when the settings first load (`kamiwaza/serving/two_node.py:156`).

Attach checks that the node answers over SSH before it saves anything (`kamiwaza/serving/two_node.py:223`). Only one paired node is supported; a second attach is refused (`kamiwaza/cluster/nodes.py:438`). SSH host-key checking is off unless the caller sets `strict_host_key_checking` (`kamiwaza/cluster/schemas/cluster.py:661`). vLLM starts a container on the paired node only when the launch targets it. `auto` stays local (`kamiwaza/serving/engines/VLLMEngine.py:3780`), and the two-node Ray launch puts the worker there by default (`kamiwaza/serving/two_node_launcher.py:372`). llama.cpp starts every container on the paired node while one is attached (`kamiwaza/serving/engines/LlamaCppEngine.py:1744`).

The path is Docker over SSH in the vLLM and llama.cpp engines. The Kubernetes engine adapters do not call the two-node runner at this revision, so support on a Kubernetes install is not established. The two-node guide was retired, and `platform.kubernetes-install` lists a published two-node topology as not supported. This document records only that the source ships the admin API and the serving path. It is not evidence of other multi-node layouts or of every GPU vendor.

capabilities.title: Ask an operations copilot grounded questions about the platform
capabilities.summary:
- **A durable, resumable run contract.** The service contract names the state machine — `running`, `waiting_for_user`, `pending_write`, and terminal states — and clients may close a run and later resume a parked one by id.
- **Writes are parked, never assumed.** Explicit write confirmation is part of the durable contract, alongside stable call ids on parked questions and writes.
- **Actions are capability-filtered and budgeted.** Action descriptors are filtered by capability, reads are executed from a registered set, and budget accounting is contracted rather than incidental.
- **Requests carry no credentials of their own.** The current user's platform authorization is forwarded to the inference route; the copilot accepts no API key. Its model is resolved from operator configuration.
- **Actions are audited with a copilot policy tag**, so work done through the copilot is distinguishable from work done directly. Each audit event names the owning user as actor and a `copilot.*` policy id (`copilot.run`, `copilot.registry.action`); the agent is not recorded as the actor (`kamiwaza/services/copilot/audit.py` at `f991d3e6`, corrected 2026-09-28 by ENG-13250).
conditions: The copilot resolves one operator-configured Kamiwaza-hosted OpenAI-compatible deployment. The base URL is operator configuration, not user input.
limits:
- **The inner loop is an acknowledged shim.** The service's own contract document marks the current loop as interim, to be replaced when the intended reasoning component lands, and enumerates exactly what must not change when it is — durable states, confirmation semantics, schemas, ownership checks, budget accounting, the one-tool-call-per-turn invariant, result-handle citation rules, and audit behavior. Read that as the maturity signal it is: the *protocol* is meant to outlive the current implementation, and the current implementation is not the claim.
- **No documentation page describes this**, and there is no SDK surface. Two classes of support, both internal to the platform repository.

capabilities.title: Install without internet access from a customer registry mirror (air-gapped)
capabilities.summary:
- obtain-release-image-list: pull the release Helm chart and read the list of images the release can deploy, optionally filtering out the GPU inference engines.
- mirror-release-by-digest: copy the chart and every listed image into the customer registry with digests unchanged, and check that each one is present.
- relocate-images-at-install: install with `global.imageRegistryPrefix` so every image the chart deploys resolves to the customer registry, and with `core.scheduler.extensionImageRelocateRegistry` so App Garden extension images are relocated when an extension deploys.
- use-bundled-local-catalog: serve the App Garden, Tool Shed and connector catalogs from the catalog packaged in the chart (`core.templates.sync.stage: LOCAL` with `localMode.enabled: true`), with the online catalog lookup turned off.
- mirror-tenant-mode-engine-images: copy the tenant-mode inference engine images the core image's engine catalog pins, by digest, to the location the prefix resolves to.
conditions: A reachable customer registry holding the mirrored release chart and images by digest, and install values that set global.imageRegistryPrefix, core.scheduler.extensionImageRelocateRegistry and the bundled LOCAL catalog.
limits:
- **Two details of the published procedure are placeholders.** The page's own TODO comments say the image list's name and location inside the chart, and the source location of the tenant-mode engine images in the release, are not fixed until the release runbook fixes them. The steps that depend on them (step 1, and the engine-image copy) are documented as intended and may change.
- **This describes a source snapshot, not a published release.** Nothing here establishes that a release registry holding the chart, `images.txt` and the images exists for 1.3.0.
- **The registry capacity figure is the only sizing stated.** About 20 GB without GPU engines. The earlier host staging-volume contract (`/var/lib`, `/tmp`, `/`) belonged to the bundle procedure and has no counterpart; node disk is covered by the general system requirements.
- **No separate offline runbook was found.** The earlier document claimed a second runbook for artifact-by-artifact verification against an immutable release or for installs driven over a managed shell. None is in the current documentation tree or in deploy at the cited revisions.
- **GreyMatter proxy image.** The release does not publish this vendor image, so the prefix does not relocate it; `global.airgap.registry.url` does.
- **Host prerequisite tools are a separate lane.** deploy's Ansible host preparation can install prerequisite tools from a bundle whose checksum and detached signature it verifies, on RHEL/Rocky only. It is cited because it is the one checksum-verified offline artifact in source, but it prepares hosts for deploy's own tooling; the published customer procedure does not use it and Kamiwaza "does not set up or modify your cluster".
- **"Air-gapped" describes the install, not the running platform.** Nothing here establishes what the platform does or does not reach at runtime.

capabilities.title: Run Kamiwaza inside a customer-operated Grey Matter service mesh
capabilities.summary:
- Select GreyMatter as the mesh and ingress provider at install time.
- Choose the listener/upstream security mode (`gslSecurity`). On the listeners core generates for routes, `spire` renders a SPIRE listener, `pki` an mTLS listener, `tls` a TLS listener and `plaintext` a listener with no security block. The chart describes the setting as the internal GreyMatter listener/upstream identity: `spire` uses SPIFFE/SPIRE identities and `pki` uses a static certificate Secret.
- Publish routes automatically as deployments are created, through the tenant GitOps branch, and withdraw them automatically when a deployment is removed -- unless route retention is in effect (OpenShift only; see Conditions and limits), in which case removed routes stay until an operator prunes them.
- Let the extension operator submit route intents for extensions with ingress enabled when it runs in GreyMatter mode (service and connector extensions stay in-cluster and get no route).
conditions: The customer already runs GreyMatter Core and its tenant configuration manager; the Kamiwaza chart does not install or manage them.
A tenant GitOps branch that GreyMatter reconciles, with credentials the route writer can push to.

Before installing the OpenShift + GreyMatter lane, the tenant's static GSL must be rendered and synchronized to that repository: the lane starts an active GreyMatter sidecar, and the install can wait on pods that cannot join the mesh. The static GSL, not the dynamic route writer, carries listeners such as the in-namespace Keycloak listener.
GreyMatter must be selected explicitly (global.mesh.provider and global.ingress.provider set to greymatter); Istio is the default everywhere.

kamiwaza-kubernetes-setup profiles/support-matrix.yaml lists openshift-greymatter as status draft with supportClaimAllowed false ('Requires confirmation on a real ARO, ROSA, or ROSA-classic target'). Its OpenShift + GreyMatter guide records a ROSA Classic test cluster (OpenShift 4.20.39, GreyMatter platform 2.4.1, PKI) built end to end on 2026-10-01 for development and CI, without naming a Kamiwaza release. The same repository's platform-matrix document lists OpenShift + GreyMatter as release-blocking and says only confirmed_on_target backs an external support statement. No source states a 1.3.0 qualification.
limits:
- **Off by default.** Istio is the default provider in the chart, in core and in the extension operator; GreyMatter is an explicit selection.
- **The default listener/upstream identity mode is not the one the OpenShift lanes use, and neither is qualified.** Both the chart and core default to `spire`. The OpenShift overlays (`kamiwaza-openshift.yaml`, `kamiwaza-tenant-routing-greymatter-openshift-pki.yaml`) set `pki` explicitly, and the setup repository's test-cluster guide builds a PKI cluster. The setup repository's SPIRE record is a partial target validation. The earlier version of this document said the setup repository calls `pki` and `spire` "the identity modes" and reports PKI "confirmed on target"; neither wording is in the setup repository at the cited revision, and both are withdrawn. The modes themselves are implemented.
- **Qualification is not established for 1.3.0.** The setup repository's machine-readable support matrix marks the OpenShift + GreyMatter target `draft` with `supportClaimAllowed: false`. Its guide records a ROSA Classic test cluster built end to end on 2026-10-01 for Kamiwaza development and CI, and says customers bring their own OpenShift and GreyMatter. Its platform-matrix document lists OpenShift + GreyMatter as release-blocking and says only `confirmed_on_target` backs an external support statement; no `confirmed_on_target` record for this target was found at the cited revision. The setup repository also says not to collapse GreyMatter and Istio into one routing story, which is why this is its own document.
- **Route retention is OpenShift-only.** The chart computes the effective flag as `global.openshift.enabled` AND `routeWriter.retainDeletedRoutes` (`charts/core/templates/scheduler/configmap.yaml:90`). The `kamiwaza-openshift.yaml` overlay sets the value true (its comment: the tenant configuration manager currently causes a short tenant-wide outage when deleting generated routes, so stale intents are retained and pruned in a controlled maintenance window). With retention in effect a removed deployment's route is kept, the writer reports it unchanged, and there is no automatic pruning job. The chart default and the generic GreyMatter overlay set it false, and on a non-OpenShift install the value has no effect either way, so routes are withdrawn automatically there.
- **Protected and bypass routes.** What is established at the cited revisions: the route-writing paths read in core's GreyMatter provider set `auth_mode` protected, explicitly or as the parameter default a caller may override (`kamiwaza/serving/routing/providers/greymatter.py:2751`, `:3026`); the extension operator posts a route intent with `auth_mode` protected, or bypass when the extension's ingress authentication is disabled; and the static GSL sends protected routes through the external-authorization filter. Two limits follow. First, the static GSL gives a route intent that carries **no** `auth_mode` — one written before ENG-6349 — the bypass default, deliberately fail-open during a rolling upgrade (`charts/network/templates/greymatter/gsl-runtime-bundle.yaml:210-226`); such routes are unauthenticated at the edge until rewritten. Second, the earlier version of this document said the direct extension runtime publishes *every* extension route as protected and that *only* the extension operator can produce a bypass route. That universal statement is not closed across all route-writing callers at the cited revisions and is withdrawn as a guarantee; it remains the intended design and is recorded as an open source-proof item.
- **Withdrawal of extension routes is best-effort on the operator side.** The operator logs a failed GreyMatter route cleanup as non-fatal, so an extension's route can outlive the extension until the next successful cleanup.
- **Automatic publication needs the writer enabled.** Routes are committed and pushed only when the route writer is enabled with auto-commit and auto-push; a disabled writer logs and skips.

capabilities.title: Install Kamiwaza on supported platforms, including multi-node clusters
capabilities.summary:
- Install by the documented two-stage process: a platform administrator prepares the cluster, then one Helm release is installed into a single namespace with a namespace-scoped installer identity.
- Size the install against the published, tiered requirements (baseline, production, GPU workloads).
- Serve models on NVIDIA GPUs (compute capability 7.0 or above) on the documented install, on GPU nodes prepared as the GPU-nodes page describes.
- Run on a multi-node cluster — one Kubernetes cluster spread over several nodes — per the multi-node section of the chosen environment's prerequisites.
- Read the running system's own inventory of locations, clusters, nodes and hardware through the API and the SDK (administrator only).
conditions: At least 8 cores; 16 or more recommended for CPU-based inference. Linux x64/amd64.
16 GB minimum for a baseline install with limited capacity for apps and tools, 32 GB for production, and 32 GB or more alongside GPU vRAM for GPU workloads.

GPU inference requires 16 GB or more of vRAM, with 32 GB or more recommended. On the documented install (Helm into one namespace, local models served through tenant-mode inference) this release serves NVIDIA GPUs only, at compute capability 7.0 or above; no ROCm engine image ships for it. AMD via ROCm and unified-memory systems are listed in the requirements page and modelled by GPU detection, but no install lane that serves on them is bound to source here.
limits:
- **AMD/ROCm and unified-memory serving is not established for any current install lane.** The earlier version of this document claimed multiple accelerator families as supported without qualification. At the cited revisions the documented install is NVIDIA only. deploy still carries AMD material (an `amd-gpu-device-plugin` chart, ROCm engine notes in the core chart values, node labels for `rocm`), which belongs to lanes other than the documented install; which lane, if any, is supported for a customer is not bound to source here. Treat AMD and unified-memory as documented-and-detectable, not as a supported serving configuration, until that is curated.
- **Two install lanes exist and only one is the customer's.** The documented customer install is Helm into a namespace of a customer-run cluster, and Kamiwaza "does not set up or modify your cluster". The deploy tooling cited in front matter (`install-dev.sh`, the prerequisites role, the join-worker play) is the developer lane that prepares k0s on macOS or Linux hosts. It is cited because it is the installer code in source; it is not the published customer procedure, and its OS and runtime dispatch are not a customer support matrix. The namespace install is described in detail in `platform.tenant-namespace-install`.
- **The two-node guide was retired.** `docs/docs/installation/two-node-deployment.md` was deliberately removed upstream as a legacy topology. The multi-node story is consequently thinner in documentation than it was, and any specific two-node claim should be re-confirmed before use.
- **The cluster inventory reports, it does not validate.** `list_nodes` and `list_hardware` show what a deployment contains. They do not establish that a multi-node install was performed correctly or that the topology is supported. The routes are administrator-only.
- **Air-gapped installation is a separate claim** with its own prerequisites — see `platform.airgapped-install`. Do not read support for one as support for the other.

capabilities.title: Install Kamiwaza with Helm into a namespace of a customer-owned Kubernetes cluster (reference target Red Hat OpenShift)
capabilities.summary:
- Prepare prerequisites (platform team, out of band) and verify them with the per-section checks of the published prerequisites page for the environment.
- Install the release with a namespace-admin identity (tenant-direct) or with administrator-granted RBAC (Extended).
- Check a rendered release against the tenant contract with deploy's render gate.
- Build a tenant OCI bundle (`complete` or `cpu-only` profile) and import it for a disconnected OpenShift install, with deploy's bundle tooling.
conditions: The customer's platform team supplies, out of band, what the setup repository's tenant contract (contracts/platform-prerequisites.v1.yaml) lists -- the namespace, OpenShift SCC bindings (on OpenShift), an RWO storage class, object storage (external S3 or external Blob; or SeaweedFS in the namespace, which the release itself renders when enabled, with its credentials Secret pre-created), an image pull secret, and the routing provider (GreyMatter or Istio) and edge -- and two more from deploy's direct-runtime lanes. First, supplemental namespaced Roles pre-bound to the Helm installer identity: a stock OpenShift namespace admin lacks atoms the release's own Roles delegate (pods/exec get among them), and Kubernetes escalation prevention then rejects those Roles. Second, where requireEgressCidrs is set (the GreyMatter sidecar routing activation overlay kamiwaza-tenant-routing-greymatter-active.yaml and the no-Istio tenant overlay; the chart default is off), the post-DNAT Kubernetes API endpoint CIDRs, without which the chart refuses to render. Apart from the in-namespace SeaweedFS option, the Kamiwaza release creates none of these; this list is assembled from those sources and is not a certified complete checklist.

Node-global kernel settings are the platform team's: the setup contract requires fs.inotify.max_user_instances >= 8192, fs.inotify.max_user_watches >= 1048576 and fs.inotify.max_queued_events >= 16384. The contract records that below the max_user_instances floor Istio sidecars crash-loop ('too many open files') once enough pods run, so an install can render and start but fail at product scale.

Tenant-direct mode grants no Node-read permission. The legacy GPU path auto-detects GPUs by listing Nodes when the chart's scheduler.gpuType is auto (the default); forcing a vendor with scheduler.gpuType skips that detection, but the deploy path still probes Nodes: a denied metadata read and a denied node-role probe are tolerated, while a denied gpu-vendor label probe keeps a kamiwaza.ai/gpu-vendor node selector, so the GPU pod schedules only on nodes carrying Kamiwaza's gpu-vendor label and stays Pending on a customer-managed cluster without it. The Node-free GPU path the kit declares is models.tenant-mode-inference (owner-signed compute profiles), which is not in the release-candidate tag db335158b; legacy GPU serving on a tenant-direct identity with a forced vendor is not established here.

Tenant-direct mode needs a namespace-admin identity plus the supplemental namespaced Roles in platform_prerequisites. Extended (operator) mode additionally needs cluster-scoped RBAC and a node-read grant, applied by an administrator.
kamiwaza-kubernetes-setup profiles/support-matrix.yaml marks every target, OpenShift + GreyMatter and HPE EZUA included, with supportClaimAllowed false; the tenant contract is status draft.
limits:
- **Tenant-direct guarantees are mode-specific.** "Only namespaced objects" and "no Node-read grant" hold for tenant-direct. In Extended mode the setup repository's contract has the administrator pre-provision the CRDs, operators and cluster RBAC, and says the chart emits no cluster-scoped objects in either mode; forbidding Node reads is a "Tenant-mode rule ONLY", and Node read is an Extended prerequisite. The EZUA overlay sits between the two: at the cited deploy revision it uses the direct runtime and enables no operator, but as shipped it creates a cluster-scoped node-reader role and binding, and deploy's CI passes it through the tenant render gate only with that creation forced off.
- **Installing is not by itself a GPU-serving claim.** The legacy GPU path auto-detects GPUs by listing Nodes (`kamiwaza/serving/engines/k8s_gpu.py` for llama.cpp and whisper.cpp; a separate implementation, `K8sVLLMAdapter.resolve_k8s_gpu_info`, for vLLM and diffusion), which a tenant-direct identity may not do; a forced vendor (`scheduler.gpuType`) skips that detection, but a denied gpu-vendor label probe keeps a `kamiwaza.ai/gpu-vendor` node selector (see preconditions), so legacy GPU serving on a tenant-direct identity needs that Kamiwaza label on the GPU nodes and is not established by these sources. The GPU path the kit declares for a Node-free install is `models.tenant-mode-inference`, which is off by default and absent from the release-candidate tag.
- **Node sysctls and object storage are platform prerequisites.** The setup contract's inotify floors (see preconditions) are node-global settings the tenant cannot change; object storage must be external or an in-namespace SeaweedFS, which the release renders (the tenant object-storage overlay sets the SeaweedFS backend) from a pre-created credentials Secret.
- **No 1.3.0 qualification.** The setup repository's support matrix marks every target `supportClaimAllowed: false`. At the cited deploy revision the OpenShift + GreyMatter tenant lane is a stack of overlays; the single lane file that described itself as the ROSA14 validation contract and used `release-1.1.0` branch images no longer exists, so those statements are withdrawn rather than carried forward. The bring-your-own-Istio overlay still says production customer installs should pin its image tags by digest during artifact promotion. HPE EZUA is a documentation-only secondary target in the setup repository.
- **Explicit configuration.** The platform and routing provider are chosen by values; nothing is auto-detected.
- **The render gate's list is a list.** It refuses the 20 kinds it names; a cluster-scoped kind outside the list would not be caught by that check.

capabilities.title: Run asynchronous retrieval jobs with streaming results
capabilities.summary:
- create-job
- get-job-status
- list-jobs
- cancel-job
- stream-job-sse
- fetch-flight-batches
- sdk-materialize
conditions: The target is a catalog dataset identified by URN; the caller holds viewer (or higher) access to it, and when ReBAC is enabled the dataset `can_view` check gates create, status, and stream.
Job creation runs under a workroom read context; the job records its workroom and tenant at create time.

The gRPC transport requires network reachability to the platform's Arrow Flight endpoint (port 6130 by default) with TLS. The Flight server refuses to start without a certificate and key unless insecure mode is explicitly allowed.

Offset, filters and ordering are accepted only on the governed record-query route (POST /retrieval/query-jobs), which has its own closed request contract and does not offer the grpc transport. POST /retrieval/jobs rejects them.
limits:
- Retrieval is dataset-addressed, not connector-addressed: the job targets a catalog URN, and the adapter behind the dataset does the reading. A source with no registered dataset is not retrievable through this surface.
- Kafka datasets cannot be materialized through the SDK yet — the SDK rejects Kafka URNs client-side before job creation.
- The SDK has no cancel method; cancellation exists only on the REST API at the pinned revision.
- **Offset, filters and ordering are not part of this job route.** At Core develop `4d00746` they belong to `POST /retrieval/query-jobs`, a separate governed record-query surface with required ordering and limit, no `grpc` transport and its own stream route. That surface is not claimed by this document and the SDK does not wrap it.
- **The SDK request model is wider than the server contract.** `kamiwaza_sdk` `RetrievalRequest` still declares `offset` and `filters`. A caller who sets either gets the server's 422 as a typed SDK error; the call does not silently drop the field. Core revisions before the record-query split (Core commit `dbb85c2850`, ENG-10407) declared those two fields on this route's request model, so an SDK caller that sets them fails against develop `4d00746`; which released versions sit on either side of that commit was not established here. Reconciling the SDK model with the server contract is open and owned by the SDK.
- Non-admin callers, and callers arriving over the mesh, list only their own jobs; a native admin lists all. Status, cancel and stream are owner-checked.
- `materialize` is an SDK-side convenience; the server exposes no materialize endpoint.
- The docs page describes the bulk transport as a named gRPC service (`RetrievalService.StreamData`); the code at the pinned revision ships Arrow Flight with single-use DoGet tickets instead, and the docs also omit the cancel endpoint, the status vocabulary, and the managed-dataset adapter. Where they disagree, this document follows the code.

capabilities.title: Curate and share reusable agent skills in a platform skills library
capabilities.summary:
- **Import draft.** Validate and import a raw Agent Skills package or one-entry snapshot as draft.
- **List and filter.** List tenant-visible skills using search, category, tag, status and pagination.
- **Curate metadata.** Update allowed metadata while preserving stored package bytes.
- **Change lifecycle.** Publish, archive and restore to draft under the allowed transition rules.
- **Download published package.** Download the original source ZIP for an authorized published skill.
- **Export single snapshot.** Export one v2 snapshot preserving package checksum and current metadata.
- **Export filtered bundle.** Export the matching selection as a v2 multi-entry ZIP bundle.
- **Soft-delete.** Delete idempotently, hide later reads, retain backing history.
conditions: The caller holds the skills read context for listing and the skills write context for import, edit, export, and delete.
A skill package is a ZIP containing a SKILL.md with YAML front matter, optionally with scripts, assets, and references directories.
limits:
- Read and write are separately gated (skills read context versus write context); import, metadata edits, export bundles, and deletion all require the write context.
- The library shares skills; it does not execute them. How a consuming application (for example Kaizen custom agents) activates a published skill is that surface's claim, not this one.
- A stored skill is two artifacts, not one: a `skill_library` row and an object-storage prefix (the row's `storage_path`) holding `package.zip` alongside a derived `content.md` and `manifest.json`. `storage_path` is deliberately not exposed by the API. The row's `content_checksum` is the SHA-256 of the uploaded package bytes.
- Import validates package structure (the `SKILL.md` with YAML front matter contract); it does not certify the behavior of the skill's contents — curation and classification of what is fit to enable remain human decisions the metadata fields exist to record.

capabilities.title: Create a workroom
capabilities.summary:
- **Self-service creation with the creator as owner.** An authenticated user with room-creation permission creates a workroom via `POST /workrooms/` (201) and is recorded as its owner; ownership assignment happens during persistence, and the owner relation tuple is additionally assigned best-effort after commit. Users without the required role receive 403; the per-user active-workroom limit (operator-configurable, default 50) returns 409 when exceeded.
- **A choice of persistence posture at creation.** `type` is `ephemeral` or `persistent`. Ephemeral (shown as "Temporary" in the UI) workrooms are cleaned up automatically: a session-teardown purge deletes a still-eligible ephemeral workroom when the owning session ends, and a recurring cleanup task auto-purges ephemeral workrooms after an operator-configurable timeout (default 24 hours). Persistent workrooms remain until explicitly deleted. The type cannot be changed after creation.
- **Descriptive metadata on the create call.** Name (1–255 characters), optional description, freeform labels, a classification label, extensible key-value attributes, and SCG reference strings are all accepted on the same `POST /workrooms/` call and through the SDK. UI coverage is narrower: the built-in core Workroom Manager's create dialog is a single step accepting name, type, and description only, so labels and classification are set through the API or SDK. (The two-step wizard that also collected labels and classification belonged to the standalone Workroom Manager extension, which is deprecated.) `attributes` and `scg_references` are API/SDK-only — the built-in core dialog does not expose them.
- **Workroom-scoped context resources are auto-provisioned after creation.** With the default `eager` provisioning mode, creation dispatches provisioning of the workroom's scoped context resources (vector store, Graphiti, and peers); `lazy` and `disabled` modes are operator-selectable alternatives (`WORKROOM_CONTEXT_AUTO_PROVISION_MODE`). Provisioning is asynchronous and best-effort, not atomic with creation: the workroom is committed and 201 returned once the provisioners are dispatched, and a provisioner failure is logged without rolling back the workroom. A caller that needs a context resource to exist should confirm it rather than infer it from the 201.
conditions: The user is authenticated and holds a role that permits workroom creation; the platform returns 403 otherwise.
For the UI path, the Workroom Manager surface is available on the deployment (core's built-in surface; the standalone Workroom Manager extension is deprecated).
limits:
- Creation deliberately blocks non-admin writes minted from the Global Workroom context when the operator enables `WORKROOM_RESTRICT_GLOBAL_TO_ADMIN`; the route is otherwise open to any user whose roles pass the room-creation check for the tenant.
- A newly created workroom has only the creator as a member. Sharing it is a separate capability (`workrooms.membership-and-roles`).
- BYO-S3 backing for workroom storage — the external-storage half of the persistent-workroom option — is a deployment-time administrative capability documented separately as `workrooms.s3-object-storage`; the create flow itself does not configure storage backends.
- The API schema accepts a description of up to 1024 characters. (The deprecated Workroom Manager extension's wizard enforced a stricter 500-character front-end limit; core's built-in dialog does not.)

capabilities.title: Retire every workroom in an organization under a confirmed plan
capabilities.summary:
- list the organization's room inventory
- create a decommission plan (strategy, cutoff, retention contact)
- confirm a plan with the organization name
- delete the planned rooms at the cutoff (background task)
- read a room's tombstone
- read and update organization room settings (organization name, room creation policy)
conditions: The required configuration, services and permissions described below must be present.
limits:
Administrator API, with one exception: reading a room's tombstone is open to any signed-in member of the tenant. The routes are on `room_control_router`, which the console router includes (`kamiwaza/services/console/api.py:46`) and every install mounts (`kamiwaza/app.py:841`). Every route except the tombstone read requires the admin role (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_api.py:23`). No decommission happens until an administrator creates a plan: an organization with no settings row reports `decommission_state` `none` and `creation_policy` `anyone` (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:376`). Plans are scoped to the caller's tenant. The room creation policy in the settings is `anyone`, `admins` or `off` (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_schemas.py:14`): `admins` limits room creation to administrators, and `off` refuses it to everyone (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_policy.py:10`, `kamiwaza/services/console/room_policy.py:12`).

Creating a plan needs a future, timezone-aware cutoff (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:486`) and turns room creation off at once (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:500`). It stays off while the plan waits for confirmation: the settings update refuses any other creation policy while a draft plan exists (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:451`), and the room-control routes have no way to cancel a plan. The earlier policy comes back only when a confirmation with the correct organization name finds that the cutoff has passed, before or during the confirmation, and discards the expired draft (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:538`, `kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:558`, `kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:574`, `kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:598`). Confirmation needs `confirm: true` (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_schemas.py:68`) and the exact organization name from the settings (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:539`). It fails if the room inventory changed after the plan was created (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:549`). That failure leaves the draft in place, and no new plan can be created while a draft exists (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:495`): the draft can be confirmed only once the inventory matches it again, or is discarded by a correctly named confirmation after its cutoff. Room creation stays off meanwhile. While a plan is active, workroom changes return 409 (`kamiwaza/services/workrooms/api.py:706`) and room creation is refused (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_policy.py:11`). A background task started with the API looks for plans past their cutoff every 30 seconds (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:722`). At the cutoff each room is marked deleted (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_controls.py:179`), then its access relations are cleaned up and its resources scheduled for purge.

The two strategy values, `retain_then_delete` and `delete`, behave the same at this revision: rooms are archived at confirmation and deleted at the cutoff (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_schemas.py:44`). Export planning is not offered and legal-hold counts are not available (`kamiwaza/services/console/room_schemas.py:37`). Any signed-in user in the tenant can read a tombstone. Its state is `read_only` before the cutoff and `tombstone` after. The global workroom is left out of the inventory.

API only. The ui-v2 decommission page is not built into an image at this revision; the frontend image target builds `./frontend` (`docker-bake.hcl:367`), which has no decommission page.
